findings.title: Verify the installer before executing it
findings.whyItBreaks: Every build executes the bytes returned by a mutable URL as root. A changed response or a compromised upstream can modify the image that the build produces.

findings.title: Fail the Docker build when the installer download fails
findings.whyItBreaks: The pipeline returns the exit status of sh. If curl fails before writing any bytes, sh reads empty input and exits successfully, so Docker continues without running the installer. Curl also accepts HTTP error responses without a failure flag.

findings.title: Verify installer content before executing it
findings.whyItBreaks: On an uncached build, the response body from the URL or a followed redirect runs as root in the build container without a content integrity check. If the served content changes, it can alter files that ship in the image without a corresponding repository change.

findings.title: Propagate installer download failures to Docker
findings.whyItBreaks: If curl fails before returning any bytes, sh reads empty input and exits 0. With the default pipeline semantics, Docker receives that 0 and continues even though the installer never ran. Curl also lacks --fail, so an HTTP error status does not by itself cause the download command to fail.

findings.title: Verify installer integrity before executing it
findings.whyItBreaks: On an uncached build, whatever body the URL or a followed redirect returns is executed as root. The Dockerfile supplies no pinned digest or signature, so an upstream change can alter the resulting image without a repository change.

findings.title: Fail the build when the installer download fails
findings.whyItBreaks: If DNS resolution fails, curl exits nonzero without writing a script. The downstream sh receives empty input and exits zero. The pipeline returns the status of sh, so Docker continues even though the installer never ran.

findings.title: Preserve the missing-key error in LoadOrDefault

findings.title: Preserve the missing-key signal in the public lookup API

findings.title: Finish sending results before Run returns
findings.whyItBreaks: Run previously returned only after every send completed, so a caller could safely close its results channel immediately afterward. With one job and a channel buffered for one result, Run can now return before the goroutine runs. If the caller closes the channel first, the goroutine panics when it sends.

findings.title: Preserve input order in the results channel
findings.whyItBreaks: The base implementation sends results in input order. With jobs [1, 2], the worker for 2 can now send 4 before the worker for 1 sends 2. The channel carries only integers, so a caller that matches results to jobs by position can assign both results to the wrong jobs.

findings.title: Complete result sends before Run returns
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous implementation returned only after sending every result in input order. The new implementation returns after launching the senders. With one job and an unbuffered channel, a caller can call Run and then close the channel while the send is still pending, causing a send-on-closed-channel panic. With multiple jobs, sender scheduling can also reorder the results.

findings.title: Complete result sends before returning from Run
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously, Run returned only after every send completed, so the caller could safely close the results channel after Run returned. The new goroutines can send after Run returns. For example, with jobs []int{1} and an unbuffered results channel with no receiver, Run can return while the send is still pending. If the caller then closes the channel, the sending goroutine panics.

findings.title: Preserve the tenant-scoped invalidation API
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous public call invalidate(tenantId, name) now fails TypeScript argument checking. An existing JavaScript caller passes tenantId into the new name parameter, so the function deletes the key for the tenant ID as a setting name and leaves the intended entry stale.

findings.title: Keep cached settings scoped to the requesting tenant
findings.whyItBreaks: Two tenants requesting the same setting name now share one cache entry. After the first tenant's value is cached, the second tenant's request returns that value at line 14 and skips its own tenant-scoped store lookup.

findings.title: Preserve the tenant-scoped invalidation signature
findings.whyItBreaks: Existing TypeScript callers using invalidate(tenantId, name) fail to compile against the new signature. Existing JavaScript callers still pass both arguments, but the implementation treats tenantId as the setting name and ignores the second argument. If the tenant ID and setting name differ, the intended entry remains cached and subsequent reads can return stale data.

findings.title: Preserve tenant isolation in settings cache keys
findings.whyItBreaks: The module-level cache now keys entries by setting name alone. Once tenant A loads a setting, tenant B's request for the same name returns A's value at the cache-hit guard and skips the tenant-specific store fetch.

findings.title: Keep the two-argument settings invalidation API
findings.whyItBreaks: Existing TypeScript calls to invalidate(tenantId, name) fail the new arity check. Existing JavaScript callers pass both arguments, and the new implementation uses tenantId as the setting name. For invalidate('tenant-a', 'theme'), it deletes settings:tenant-a and leaves the cached settings:theme value stale.

findings.title: Make same-SKU reservations atomic across the save
findings.whyItBreaks: With one unit loaded, the first reserve call reads 1 and pauses at save(sku, 0). A second call reads the same 1 and also saves 0. Once both saves resolve, both calls return true and stock ends at 0, so two reservations are confirmed for one unit. Previously the first call decremented stock before the second call could read it.

findings.title: Serialize concurrent reservations for the same SKU
findings.whyItBreaks: With one unit in stock, two calls to reserve for the same SKU can both read 1 while the first save is pending. Both save 0, both set the in-memory count to 0, and both return true. The previous synchronous method completed the decrement before the second call could read the count.

findings.title: Preserve the existing Inventory constructor and reserve contract
findings.whyItBreaks: Existing TypeScript callers using new Inventory() now fail to compile. Callers that supply a Store but keep using reserve in a synchronous conditional enter the success branch even for an out-of-stock SKU because a Promise that resolves to false is still truthy.

findings.title: Serialize reservations for the same SKU
findings.whyItBreaks: With one unit in stock, the first reserve call reads 1 and suspends at save. A second call for the same SKU still reads 1 and also calls save with 0. When both saves resolve, both reservations return true even though only one unit was available. The previous synchronous implementation updated stock before the second call could read it.

findings.title: Preserve retry delays when changing backoff units
findings.whyItBreaks: backoff now returns milliseconds, but retry still multiplies its result by 1,000 before passing it to the millisecond timer. After the first failed attempt, the next attempt waits 1,000 seconds instead of 1 second. At attempt index 5, the delay rises from 30 seconds to 8 hours and 20 minutes.

findings.title: Remove the extra milliseconds conversion from job retries
findings.whyItBreaks: The retry caller still multiplies backoff by 1,000 before passing it to sleep, which forwards milliseconds directly to setTimeout. After the first failure, the retry waits 1,000 seconds instead of 1 second. At attempt index 5, the delay is 30,000 seconds instead of 30 seconds.

findings.title: Remove the extra seconds-to-milliseconds conversion in job retries
findings.whyItBreaks: backoff now returns milliseconds, but retry still multiplies its result by 1,000 before passing it to setTimeout. After the first failed attempt, retry waits 1,000,000 ms instead of 1,000 ms. At the cap it waits 30,000,000 ms instead of 30,000 ms.

findings.title: Propagate close errors after a successful flush
findings.whyItBreaks: If Flush returns nil and Close returns an error, Save returns nil because the deferred call discards the Close result. The public API previously returned that error, so callers lose the ability to distinguish this failure from a successful save.

findings.title: Propagate file close errors from Save
findings.whyItBreaks: When Flush returns nil and Close returns an error, the deferred call discards the close error and Save returns nil. The previous implementation returned the close error, so callers could detect a failed save.

findings.title: Propagate close failures from Save
findings.whyItBreaks: If the buffered writes flush successfully but the filesystem reports a delayed write error on close, Save returns nil. The base implementation returned the close error, so callers could detect the failed save.

findings.title: Include the last row of each page
findings.whyItBreaks: _window_bounds already returns an exclusive end. Subtracting one again drops the final row of every nonempty page. For rows=['a', 'b'], page_index=0, and page_size=2, the loop visits only position 0, so render_page prints only '1. a'. A one-row page renders as an empty string.

findings.title: Preserve existing keyword arguments for pagination helpers
findings.whyItBreaks: The base signature accepts page_count(total=3, size=2) and returns 2. The new signature rejects that call with TypeError before entering the body. The same signature change breaks the old keyword names on clamp (line 1), page_window (line 24), render_page (line 38), and summarize (line 47).

findings.title: Include the final row of each page
findings.whyItBreaks: The page end is already exclusive. For rows ['a', 'b', 'c'] and page size 2, the first page uses range(0, 1) and drops 'b'. The second page uses range(2, 2) and drops 'c'. render_page and summarize both omit those rows from their output.

findings.title: Preserve existing pagination keyword arguments
findings.whyItBreaks: The base signature accepts page_count(total=10, size=5) and returns 2. The new signature raises TypeError during argument binding. The same incompatibility affects clamp(n=1, lo=0, hi=2), page_window(rows=['a'], page=0, size=1), render_page(rows=['a'], page=0, size=1), and summarize(rows=['a'], size=1) at lines 1, 24, 38, and 47. Internal positional calls do not exercise this interface.

findings.title: Include the last row of every page
findings.whyItBreaks: _window_bounds returns an exclusive end, and range already excludes its stop. Subtracting one omits the last row of every nonempty page. A one-row page becomes empty, so render_page and summarize omit that row entirely.

findings.title: Preserve public pagination keyword arguments
findings.whyItBreaks: The base signature accepts summarize(rows=['a'], size=1). The new signature rejects size with TypeError before the body runs. The same binding regression affects clamp(n=..., lo=..., hi=...), page_count(total=..., size=...), page_window(rows=..., page=..., size=...), and render_page(rows=..., page=..., size=...). The in-repo calls are positional, so they do not exercise this compatibility break.

findings.title: Return fresh cache entries and evict expired entries
findings.whyItBreaks: With a 100 ms TTL, a lookup at age 50 ms deletes the entry and returns null. A first lookup at age 101 ms returns the expired value and leaves it cached.

findings.title: Remove every completed job, including adjacent jobs
findings.whyItBreaks: For two adjacent completed jobs, removing the first shifts the second to index 0. forEach advances to index 1 and never checks the second job, so the returned queue still contains it.

findings.title: Preserve the input array during queue pruning
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous implementation returned a new array. Splicing the input now removes completed jobs from every reference the caller holds to the original array. A single completed job is enough to observe the regression.

findings.title: Restore the TTL comparison for cache hits
findings.whyItBreaks: With a 100 ms TTL, a first read at age 0 ms deletes the entry and returns null. A first read at age 101 ms returns the expired value and leaves it cached, so later reads can keep serving it.

findings.title: Remove every completed job when pruning
findings.whyItBreaks: For two consecutive completed jobs, removing the first at index 0 shifts the second into index 0. forEach advances to index 1, leaving the second completed job in the returned queue.

findings.title: Preserve the input array when pruning jobs
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous implementation preserved the input and returned a fresh array. With one completed job and one pending job, pruneDone now removes the completed job from the caller’s array and returns that same array. Any reference the caller kept to the input observes the removal.

findings.title: Restore the cache freshness check
findings.whyItBreaks: With a 100 ms TTL, a lookup at age 50 ms deletes the entry and returns null. If the first lookup is at age 101 ms, it returns the expired value and leaves it cached.

findings.title: Remove every completed job
findings.whyItBreaks: When two completed jobs are adjacent, removing the first shifts the second into the index already visited. The next forEach iteration advances past it, so pruneDone returns a completed job.

findings.title: Preserve the caller's job array
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous implementation returned a new array and preserved the input. The changed implementation removes jobs from the caller's array and returns that same array. A caller that retains the input loses completed jobs from its original list.

findings.title: Preserve the zero average for empty input
findings.whyItBreaks: The deleted guard returned 0 for an empty array. The reduction still starts at 0, so empty input now reaches the division as 0 / 0 and the exported function returns NaN.

findings.title: Preserve the caller’s row order when selecting the busiest row
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.sort mutates its receiver. Passing rows with amounts [1, 2] now returns the second row and leaves the caller’s array ordered [2, 1]. The previous implementation sorted a copy and preserved the input order.

findings.title: Preserve the zero result for an empty average
findings.whyItBreaks: The deleted guard at base line 7 returned 0 for an empty array. With the guard gone, the reducer returns its initial value of 0 and the function divides it by the array length of 0, returning NaN to callers.

findings.title: Preserve the caller's row order in busiest
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.sort mutates the supplied array. Passing rows with amounts [1, 2] now leaves the caller's rows ordered [2, 1]. The base implementation sorted a copy and returned the same highest-amount row while preserving input order.

findings.title: Preserve the zero result for an empty average
findings.whyItBreaks: The public function accepts an empty array. At base it returned 0. The new implementation reduces the empty array to 0 and divides by its length, also 0, returning NaN. Any arithmetic using that result propagates NaN.

findings.title: Preserve caller row order when selecting the busiest row
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.prototype.sort mutates its receiver. Calling busiest on rows ordered [low, high] returns high and changes the caller’s array to [high, low]. The previous implementation sorted a copy, so callers could reuse the original order.

findings.title: Restore descending numeric sorting before selecting the cutoff
findings.whyItBreaks: Without a comparator, Array.sort orders numbers by their string representations. For scores [9, 10, 11] and n=2, reversing that order yields [9, 11, 10]. The cutoff becomes 11, so topPlayers returns only the player with 11 and formatBoard prints one row. The previous numeric sort used a cutoff of 10 and returned both qualifying players.

findings.title: Sort leaderboard scores numerically before selecting the cutoff
findings.whyItBreaks: JavaScript's default sort compares scores as strings. With players A (9) and B (10) in that order and n=1, reversing the sorted scores gives [9, 10]. The cutoff becomes 9, both players pass the filter, and slice returns A. formatBoard displays A in first place.

findings.title: Sort leaderboard scores in descending numeric order
findings.whyItBreaks: Default JavaScript sorting compares scores as strings. For players listed with scores 9 and 10 and n=1, reversing the sorted scores produces [9, 10]. The cutoff becomes 9, both players pass the filter, and slice(0, 1) returns the player who scored 9. formatBoard then displays that player in first place. The base version selects the player who scored 10.

findings.title: Restore timing-resistant webhook signature comparison
findings.whyItBreaks: Ordinary string equality can take different amounts of time depending on the contents of the supplied signature and the secret-derived HMAC. This removes the timing resistance previously provided by hmac.compare_digest from the check that controls whether the webhook payload reaches the processor.

findings.title: Restore timing-resistant webhook signature comparison
findings.whyItBreaks: Ordinary string equality can take different amounts of time depending on where the supplied signature differs from the secret-derived digest. The webhook handler calls this comparison before returning 401 or invoking the processor, exposing a timing side channel in authentication.

findings.title: Restore timing-safe comparison for webhook signatures
findings.whyItBreaks: Python string equality provides no constant-time guarantee. It compares the expected HMAC against a caller-supplied signature on the authentication path, so comparison timing can reveal information about the expected signature. The result controls whether the handler invokes the payload processor.

findings.title: Keep both balance updates inside the ledger transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: The transaction exits after inserting the ledger row. If the first balance update raises on a top-level transfer, the error reaches the caller after the ledger row has committed, leaving a recorded transfer with both balances unchanged.

findings.title: Keep both balance updates inside the ledger transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: The transaction commits the ledger insert before either balance update runs. If the debit raises, the caller receives an error while the ledger still records the transfer and both balances remain unchanged. If the credit raises after the debit succeeds, the debit is also outside the transaction that protected all three writes in the base revision.

findings.title: Keep both balance updates in the ledger transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: The transaction exits successfully after the ledger insert. If the first balance update then raises, transfer returns an error after committing the ledger entry, with neither balance updated. The base implementation rolled back the ledger entry on that same failure.

findings.title: Keep billing-day calculations in UTC
findings.whyItBreaks: The local date getters can assign the same timestamp to different billing days on different hosts. In America/Los_Angeles, 2025-01-01T00:30:00Z now maps to 2024-12-31, while 2025-01-01T08:30:00Z maps to 2025-01-01. The base version maps both timestamps to 2025-01-01, so sameBillingDay changes from true to false.

findings.title: Preserve UTC when computing billing days
findings.whyItBreaks: Under America/Los_Angeles, 2026-01-01T00:30:00Z now maps to 2025-12-31 instead of 2026-01-01. Comparing it with 2026-01-01T08:30:00Z makes sameBillingDay return false for two timestamps that share a UTC billing day.

findings.title: Keep billing-day keys in UTC
findings.whyItBreaks: The local date getters change the key for the same instant across hosts. For 2025-03-02T00:30:00Z, the base implementation returns 2025-03-02 everywhere, while the new implementation returns 2025-03-01 in America/Los_Angeles. This also makes sameBillingDay return true for 2025-03-01T23:30:00Z and 2025-03-02T00:30:00Z on that host, even though the two instants fall on different UTC billing days.

findings.title: Scope cached profiles by tenant and account
findings.whyItBreaks: After readProfile caches a profile for tenant-a and account alex, a request for tenant-b and account alex uses the same key. The cache hit returns tenant-a’s profile before fetchProfile can resolve tenant-b’s account.

findings.title: Key cached profiles by tenant and account
findings.whyItBreaks: The module-wide cache uses the same entry for two tenants with the same account identifier. After one tenant's profile is cached, a read for the other tenant returns that cached profile and skips the tenant-scoped fetch. The returned profile exposes the first tenant's identifier and display name.

findings.title: Scope profile cache keys to the tenant
findings.whyItBreaks: The module-level cache is shared across calls. After readProfile caches a profile for tenant-a and account alice, a call for tenant-b and account alice hits the same entry and returns tenant-a's profile before fetchProfile can resolve the request for tenant-b.

findings.title: Preserve lookup errors in the public store loaders
findings.whyItBreaks: The catch converts both the explicit missing-key error and any exception from store.get into an empty string. loadAll therefore returns [""] for a missing key, exactly as it does for a key whose stored value is an empty string. Previously the error reached the caller and aborted the batch.

findings.title: Propagate lookup failures from load
findings.whyItBreaks: A missing key previously threw an error that propagated through loadAll. With a store containing only ['empty', ''], loadAll(['empty', 'missing'], store) now returns ['', '']. The caller cannot tell which key was absent. The catch also suppresses any exception thrown by store.get.

findings.title: Preserve missing-key errors from load
findings.whyItBreaks: The catch converts the missing-key exception into an empty string, which is also a valid stored value. With an empty map, loadAll(["a"], store) now returns [""] where it previously threw. That result is identical to loading a key explicitly set to an empty string. The catch also suppresses exceptions from store.get.

findings.title: Preserve timeoutMs for existing retry callers
findings.whyItBreaks: A previously valid Config such as { maxAttempts: 3, timeoutMs: 100 } now fails TypeScript checking because retries and timeout are required. An existing JavaScript caller passing the same object computes a NaN deadline, so the deadline check stays false even after the configured timeout has elapsed.

findings.title: Reuse retry's attempt policy for the background entry point
findings.whyItBreaks: The new function duplicates retry's deadline and exception-handling loop but counts total attempts against retries instead of maxAttempts. With { maxAttempts: 1, retries: 0, timeout: 100 } and a clock within the deadline, retry invokes the callback once while retryBackground skips the initial attempt entirely.

findings.title: Defer callback execution in retryBackground
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported name promises background execution, but the function calls fn on the caller's stack before returning. A slow callback blocks the caller, and callback side effects occur before the caller can continue.

findings.title: Expose terminal failures from retryBackground
findings.whyItBreaks: With retries set to 1 and the deadline still open, a callback that throws produces the same normal undefined result as a callback that succeeds. The exported API gives callers no completion result or error signal to distinguish success from exhausted retries.

findings.title: Preserve the existing retry configuration
findings.whyItBreaks: Existing TypeScript callers that pass { maxAttempts: 2, timeoutMs: 10 } no longer satisfy Config. Existing JavaScript callers passing the same object get a NaN deadline because config.timeout is undefined. The deadline comparison is then always false, so retry can start another attempt after the caller's original timeout.

findings.title: Expose callback failure if retryBackground remains public
findings.whyItBreaks: With retries set to 1 and a deadline that permits the first attempt, a callback that throws is caught and the function returns undefined after the loop. A callback that succeeds also returns undefined at line 26. The new public API gives callers the same result for success and exhausted retries.

findings.title: Preserve the existing retry configuration contract
findings.whyItBreaks: Existing TypeScript callers using { maxAttempts: 3, timeoutMs: 100 } fail type checking because Config now requires retries and timeout. Existing JavaScript callers using that object produce a NaN deadline, so retry starts another attempt even after the configured 100 ms budget expires.

findings.title: Allow the initial attempt with zero retries
findings.whyItBreaks: The public retries setting counts every invocation, including the initial attempt. With retries set to 0 and time left in the budget, the loop skips a callback that could succeed on its first invocation. With retries set to 1, a first-attempt failure consumes the entire allowance and the callback never gets its one retry.

findings.title: Expose terminal failures from retryBackground
findings.whyItBreaks: With one permitted invocation and time left in the budget, a callback that throws and a callback that succeeds both make retryBackground return undefined. A caller cannot determine whether the operation completed or every attempt failed. Deadline expiry returns the same result.

findings.title: Handle numeric values without accessing .length
findings.whyItBreaks: FieldProps now accepts numbers, but TypeScript rejects `.length` on `string | number` because `number` has no `length` property. If transpiled without type checking, `value={42}` initializes the input to `len=undefined`.

findings.title: Preserve the supplied string as the input’s initial value
findings.whyItBreaks: Mounting `<Field value="hello" />` previously initialized the editable input to `hello`. It now initializes the input to `len=5`, so the original text is absent from the field.

findings.title: Handle numeric values before reading string length
findings.whyItBreaks: FieldProps now accepts numbers, but TypeScript rejects value.length because number has no length property. If the code is transpiled without type checking, mounting Field with value={42} initializes the input to "len=undefined".

findings.title: Preserve the supplied string as the initial input value
findings.whyItBreaks: With value="hello", a newly mounted input previously contained "hello" and now contains "len=5". Users editing a prefilled field start from the length label and lose the original text from the input.

findings.title: Handle numeric values before reading length
findings.whyItBreaks: The public prop accepts string | number, but number has no length property, so TypeScript rejects the access. If the code is transpiled without type checking, value={42} initializes the input to "len=undefined".

findings.title: Preserve the supplied string as the input's initial value
findings.whyItBreaks: The base component passes the supplied string directly to defaultValue. The changed component initializes <Field value="abc" /> to "len=3", so an existing caller loses the text it supplied even if numeric handling is fixed.

findings.title: Keep the deployment token out of workflow output
findings.whyItBreaks: When secrets.TOKEN is configured, the shell expands it into the echo command and writes the full credential to the runner's output stream before masking. This puts the credential on the logging path and relies on GitHub Actions to redact it before publishing the log.

findings.title: Remove the deployment token from workflow output
findings.whyItBreaks: The shell expands TOKEN and writes its raw value to stdout. GitHub Actions normally masks registered secrets in displayed logs, but this step sends the credential into the logging pipeline and relies on redaction to prevent disclosure. The step performs no deployment operation that needs the token.

findings.title: Keep the deployment token out of step output
findings.whyItBreaks: On every push with TOKEN configured, the shell expands the secret and writes it to stdout. GitHub Actions normally masks registered secrets in published logs, so the confirmed defect is that the step sends the raw credential into the output stream and depends on downstream redaction to protect it.

findings.title: Restore the Git output buffer for large PR reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: Omitting maxBuffer lowers the Git output limit from 64 MiB to Node's 1 MiB default. A 2 MiB patch that previously reached review() now overflows the buffer and makes git() throw. Patch collection happens before the try block, so the adapter also skips its review-failure check.

findings.title: Keep the review bundle's base SHA aligned with its patch
findings.whyItBreaks: When PR_BASE_SHA differs from the merge base, review() receives a bundle whose baseSha..headSha range describes a different diff from the patch. On diverged branches, reconstructing the diff from the recorded SHAs can include reversals of target-branch changes that are absent from the PR patch.

findings.title: Preserve the Git output buffer for large PRs
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing maxBuffer lowers the Git subprocess limit from 64 MiB to Node's 1 MiB default. A textual PR diff of 1,048,577 bytes exceeds the new limit. The Git helper throws during patch collection, before the review try/catch, so the adapter neither invokes review nor posts its failure check.

findings.title: Use the patch merge base in the review bundle
findings.whyItBreaks: When PR_BASE_SHA points to a target tip that has diverged from the PR head, the patch is computed from their merge base, but review receives the target tip as bundle.baseSha. The bundle then identifies a different comparison from the one used to produce its patch. Reproducing the diff from the supplied SHAs can include reversals of target-only changes.

findings.title: Restore the Git output buffer for large PR patches
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing maxBuffer lowers Node's synchronous Git output limit from 64 MiB to 1 MiB. A 2 MiB PR diff that previously fit now causes spawnSync to fail with ENOBUFS. The helper throws during patch generation, before runGithub enters its try block, so this invocation produces neither a review nor its failure check.

findings.title: Keep the review bundle base aligned with the patch baseline
findings.whyItBreaks: When PR_BASE_SHA points to a target branch tip that advanced after the PR forked, it differs from mergeBase. The adapter still generates the patch and changed-file list from mergeBase, but now passes the target tip as the bundle's baseSha. A review consumer reconstructing the diff from the advertised endpoints would see target-only changes as removals even though those removals are absent from the supplied patch.

findings.title: Restore the read-only sandbox override
findings.whyItBreaks: The launcher passes the review prompt to Codex with the repository as its working directory. Previously it explicitly selected the read-only sandbox. With the override removed, a machine configured for workspace-write can run the review with permission to modify the checkout. The prompt's read-only instruction does not enforce filesystem permissions.

findings.title: Keep Codex reviews in a read-only sandbox
findings.whyItBreaks: The runner launches Codex with the reviewed repository as its working directory. The previous `-s read-only` flag overrode the CLI's configured sandbox mode. With that flag removed, a local `workspace-write` configuration allows the review agent to modify the checkout, including when instructions embedded in reviewed content induce a write.

findings.title: Keep Codex reviews in a read-only sandbox
findings.whyItBreaks: The wrapper launches Codex with the reviewed repository as its working directory. Removing `-s read-only` lets the local Codex configuration select the sandbox. On a machine configured for workspace writes, a review can now modify files in that repository. The previous invocation explicitly enforced read-only access.

findings.title: Review the commit identified by PR_HEAD_SHA
findings.whyItBreaks: When PR_HEAD_SHA differs from the checkout, the adapter reviews the checkout's patch but posts the verdict and inline line numbers against PR_HEAD_SHA. A stale checkout can omit changes from the commit that receives the check. A newer checkout can introduce findings for changes absent from that commit.

findings.title: Start the PR diff at the merge base
findings.whyItBreaks: When PR_BASE_SHA identifies a target branch tip that has advanced since the PR forked, comparing the two tips makes target-only changes appear as reversions in the PR patch. Those files also enter changedPaths, so the adapter can report findings and attempt inline comments on files the PR never touched.

findings.title: Use the configured PR head for both diff inputs
findings.whyItBreaks: PR_HEAD_SHA still determines which commit receives the review and check, but the patch and changed-file list now come from the checkout's HEAD. If HEAD is a CI merge commit or a different checkout, the adapter can publish a passing check for a PR head whose patch it never reviewed. Inline finding coordinates can also refer to the wrong tree.

findings.title: Compare the PR against its merge base
findings.whyItBreaks: With HEAD at the PR head and PR_BASE_SHA at the tip of an independently advanced base branch, the direct comparison treats files added only on the base branch as PR deletions. Those deletions enter both the patch and the changed-file list and can lead to a changes-requested review for changes outside the PR.

findings.title: Use the merge base to isolate changes introduced by the PR
findings.whyItBreaks: When PR_BASE_SHA points to a target branch that advanced after the PR forked, comparing its tree directly with the PR head makes target-only additions look like PR deletions. The adapter puts those hunks and paths into the review bundle, so findings can be attributed to a PR that never touched those files.

findings.title: Build the review inputs from the commit receiving the verdict
findings.whyItBreaks: PR_HEAD_SHA still sets the bundle's head and the commit that receives the GitHub review and check, but the patch now uses local HEAD. If local HEAD equals the base and PR_HEAD_SHA contains changes, the adapter sends an empty patch and file list to review while posting the verdict on the changed PR commit. Before this change, the patch still contained the PR commit's hunks.

findings.title: Preserve literal content when inserting review prompt data
findings.whyItBreaks: JavaScript expands replacement tokens such as `$&` and `$$` when the second argument to `String.replace` is a string. A changed line containing `$&` reaches the reviewer with `{{BUNDLE}}` in its place and reaches the critic with `{{PATCH}}` in its place. The same substitution rewrites `$&` in candidate findings to `{{FINDINGS}}`. Both passes can therefore assess different text from the actual diff or finding.

findings.title: Preserve literal patch and finding text in review prompts
findings.whyItBreaks: JavaScript interprets $& in a string replacement as the matched text. A patch adding `return text.replace(pattern, '[$&]')` therefore reaches the reviewer with `[{{BUNDLE}}]` and the critic with `[{{PATCH}}]` in the quoted code. The findings substitution likewise rewrites any quoted `$&` to `{{FINDINGS}}`. The reviewer and critic can assess different code from what the PR actually changes.

findings.title: Preserve literal review data during prompt substitution
findings.whyItBreaks: JavaScript interprets replacement tokens in string arguments to replace. A valid diff containing the literal sequence $& is sent to the reviewer with that sequence changed to {{BUNDLE}} and to the critic with it changed to {{PATCH}}. The same sequence in a candidate finding becomes {{FINDINGS}}. Both stages can therefore evaluate text that differs from the actual diff or candidate findings.

findings.title: Keep fallback reviews pinned to the reviewed commit
findings.whyItBreaks: Needlefish builds the diff against a fixed head SHA. If GitHub rejects the inline review and the PR has advanced, the fallback omits commit_id. GitHub then associates the review with the latest PR commit. This can post REQUEST_CHANGES against unreviewed code while the corresponding check remains attached to the older commit.

findings.title: Keep fallback reviews pinned to the reviewed commit
findings.whyItBreaks: If the PR advances from commit A to commit B during analysis and the inline review request fails, the fallback omits commit_id. GitHub defaults it to the latest PR commit, so it attaches the review of A to B. A REQUEST_CHANGES verdict can therefore reach the new head based solely on findings from the old diff, while the check run still targets A.

findings.title: Keep the fallback review pinned to the reviewed commit
findings.whyItBreaks: If the inline review POST fails and the PR has advanced from commit A to commit B, the fallback omits commit_id. GitHub defaults an omitted commit_id to the latest PR commit, so the fallback can post a REQUEST_CHANGES review against B using findings computed from A. The check run still targets A.

findings.title: Reject malformed findings before returning a review
findings.whyItBreaks: A review containing findings: [{}] previously threw a validation error. It now returns a P1 bug with an empty file, line range 0–0, and no explanation or fix. Invalid numeric strings also survive as NaN. The public API returns these entries in the same findings array as valid results, with no failure signal.

findings.title: Trim category values before enum validation
findings.whyItBreaks: An otherwise valid finding with category ' security ' previously normalized to 'security'. The new membership check uses the raw value, so normalizeReview returns the same finding classified as 'bug'. Restoring rejection alone would still reject input that previously worked.

findings.title: Preserve tolerant review normalization
findings.whyItBreaks: The public normalizeReview(raw, false) call previously discarded a null finding and returned the valid findings in the same batch. The new signature rejects the second argument in TypeScript, and an existing JavaScript caller supplying false now gets a TypeError on null, losing the entire review result.

findings.title: Reject malformed findings before applying defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: An empty object in a review's findings array previously raised an invalid-severity error in the default mode. It now reaches RawReview.findings as a P1 bug with an empty file and a 0–0 line range. The caller receives an unlocatable finding with a severity the input never supplied. Explicit invalid ranges also pass through, including NaN for lineStart: "abc".

findings.title: Preserve lenient review normalization for existing callers
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported normalizeReview(raw, false) call previously skipped a null finding and returned the other findings. Removing the second parameter breaks existing typed calls. At runtime the unconditional map reads null.severity and throws, so callers using the old lenient invocation lose the entire review.

findings.title: Preserve validation errors for malformed findings
findings.whyItBreaks: A review with findings: [{}] now returns a P1 bug with an empty file, line range 0–0, and no explanation or fix. The previous default parser threw. An invalid severity now becomes indistinguishable from an explicitly supplied P1, and a category such as " security " that previously normalized to "security" now silently becomes "bug".

findings.title: Keep the exported lenient review parser compatible
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported normalizeReview(raw, false) call no longer type-checks. In JavaScript, the second argument is ignored. With findings: [null, validFinding], the old lenient call returned the valid sibling, while the new call throws when normalizeFinding reads null.severity.

findings.title: Restore explicit repository targeting for manual PR lookup
findings.whyItBreaks: Manual dispatch supplies a PR number and leaves EVENT_HEAD empty, so both gh commands run before the first checkout. On a clean runner workspace with no Git repository and no GH_REPO override, gh cannot resolve the repository. The enclosing echo commands mask the lookup exit statuses and write empty refs. Checkout then falls back to the dispatch ref and the review step receives empty PR SHA variables.

findings.title: Specify the repository when resolving manual PR refs
findings.whyItBreaks: A manual dispatch has no pull-request event SHAs, so it runs both numeric `gh pr view` lookups before any checkout. On a clean self-hosted workspace, `gh` cannot infer the repository without `-R`. The surrounding `echo` commands mask those failures and write empty outputs. Checkout then falls back to the dispatch ref and SHA, and the review step receives empty PR SHAs.

findings.title: Resolve manual PR refs against the workflow repository
findings.whyItBreaks: A workflow_dispatch event has no pull_request.head.sha, so it takes the gh lookup branch before actions/checkout runs. Removing -R makes gh depend on the runner's local Git context. A clean workspace has no Git remote to resolve, and a retained workspace can point to another repository. When gh fails before returning a SHA, the surrounding echo succeeds and publishes an empty output. Checkout then uses the dispatch event ref, which may differ from the requested PR head.

findings.title: Preserve validation errors for malformed review output
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported normalizer previously threw when a required top-level field was missing or had the wrong type. A payload with findings stored as an object containing a P1 finding, or residual_risks stored as an object containing blocks: true, now returns an empty array for that field. The returned RawReview carries no signal that the input failed validation, so a caller cannot distinguish discarded review data from a valid empty result.

findings.title: Reject malformed review output before normalizing it
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported normalizer used to throw when the review was missing or a required field had the wrong type. It now returns a RawReview even when findings or residual_risks are malformed. For example, a blocking risk supplied as a single object is replaced with an empty array, producing the same result as an explicit declaration of zero risks. The return value gives callers no way to distinguish those cases.

findings.title: Preserve validation errors for malformed review output
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported normalizer previously threw when the payload or any required top-level field was malformed. It now returns the same value for null as for {"summary":"","findings":[],"checked":[],"residual_risks":[]}. It also turns a single blocking risk supplied as an object into an empty risks array. Callers lose the error signal and cannot distinguish malformed output from a valid review with no findings or risks.

findings.title: Check out the requested PR head on manual dispatch
findings.whyItBreaks: A workflow_dispatch event supplies the requested PR number but has no pull_request payload. The checkout therefore selects github.ref, while the review command still receives the requested PR number. When the dispatch ref and PR head differ, the workflow installs dependencies and runs src/cli.ts from the dispatch ref. The previous workflow resolved the requested PR's head SHA before checkout.

findings.title: Resolve the requested PR refs before checking out a manual review
findings.whyItBreaks: A workflow_dispatch event supplies a PR number but no pull_request payload. If an operator dispatches from main to review a PR whose head differs from main, checkout selects refs/heads/main. The install and review steps then run from main, and the review CLI receives empty PR_BASE_SHA and PR_HEAD_SHA values. Before this change, the workflow resolved both SHAs from the requested PR and ran the reviewer from that PR's head.

findings.title: Avoid requiring a live base branch after full-history checkout
findings.whyItBreaks: On a rerun, the pull_request payload retains the original base branch name. If that branch has since been deleted while the recorded base and head commits remain reachable, checkout can still succeed and both pinned SHAs can be reviewed. The added fetch nevertheless fails because the old refs/heads/<base> no longer exists, so the workflow stops before review.

findings.title: Check out the selected PR head on manual dispatch
findings.whyItBreaks: A workflow_dispatch event supplies a PR number and a dispatch ref, but has no pull_request payload. If the dispatch ref is refs/heads/main and the selected PR has a different head commit, checkout selects main. The install and review steps then use the dispatch branch's tree, breaking the workflow's stated self-review behavior of running the selected PR's own source.

findings.title: Preserve the Git buffer limit for large local reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing the explicit 64 MiB maxBuffer makes spawnSync use Node's 1 MiB default. A successful Git diff that emits 2 MiB previously fit in the buffer. The same diff now exceeds the limit, terminates the subprocess, and makes the status check throw. The call in runLocal propagates that exception before it can submit the patch for review.

findings.title: Preserve the Git output buffer for large local reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing maxBuffer lowers the Git output limit from 67,108,864 bytes to Node’s default of 1,048,576 bytes. For example, a successful 2 MiB textual diff fits the old limit but exceeds the new one. When spawnSync terminates Git for exceeding the buffer, the status guard throws and runLocal never sends the patch to review.

findings.title: Preserve the Git output buffer for large local reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: Omitting maxBuffer makes Node's spawnSync use its 1 MiB default instead of the previous 64 MiB limit. A Git diff with 2 MiB of stdout now exceeds the buffer and returns an ENOBUFS error with a null status. The status check throws before runLocal can build the review bundle or call review.

findings.title: Scope the PR diff request to the repository being reviewed
findings.whyItBreaks: The metadata request and review submission use GITHUB_REPOSITORY. The new `gh pr diff` command has no `--repo`, and `ghText` starts it in the process working directory, ignoring the checkout passed as `cwd`. If the process runs from another repository with the same PR number, the adapter can review that repository's patch and submit the resulting approval to the intended PR.

findings.title: Use one PR revision for the patch, changed files, and review
findings.whyItBreaks: The patch comes from the live PR, the changed-file list comes from local `HEAD`, and the review commit comes from a separate metadata request. Rerun an older checkout after a push that adds `new.ts`: the patch contains `new.ts`, but `changedPaths.has('new.ts')` is false, so the adapter drops any inline finding for that file. If a push lands between the metadata and diff requests, the adapter can also submit a verdict for a patch belonging to a different commit.

findings.title: Keep failed reviews blocking when Needlefish is required
findings.whyItBreaks: GitHub accepts a completed check with a `neutral` conclusion for required status checks. If `review(bundle)` throws and `Needlefish` is the required check, the new conclusion satisfies that merge requirement despite there being no review verdict. The error summary and process exit code do not change the conclusion of the separately posted `Needlefish` check.

findings.title: Report PR diff retrieval failures through the check status
findings.whyItBreaks: The new network call has a failure path before the `try` block. If the PR metadata request succeeds and `gh pr diff` returns a nonzero status, `ghText` throws after `headSha` is known, but the adapter never reaches the error handler that publishes the completed `Needlefish` check. A required check can remain expected without a check result explaining the failure.

findings.title: Pin the patch, changed paths, and verdict to one PR revision
findings.whyItBreaks: The metadata request fixes headSha at commit A, but the subsequent PR-number diff resolves the current head independently. If a push lands between the requests, the reviewer sees commit B's patch while postReview and postCheck attach its verdict to A. The changed-file list also comes from local HEAD, so when the checkout stays at A and B adds a file, inlineComments drops any finding on that file.

findings.title: Scope the PR diff request to the publishing repository
findings.whyItBreaks: Metadata and review publication target GITHUB_REPOSITORY explicitly. The new gh pr diff call lets GitHub CLI resolve the repository from its own context, including GH_REPO. If GH_REPO points to a different repository with the same PR number, the patch comes from that repository while the approval and check are published to GITHUB_REPOSITORY.

findings.title: Keep errored reviews failing the Needlefish check
findings.whyItBreaks: GitHub accepts a neutral conclusion for a required status check. If Needlefish is required and review throws, the posted check can satisfy that merge requirement without a completed review. The failure summary and nonzero process exit remain visible, but neither changes the conclusion of the separately published Needlefish check.

findings.title: Keep execution failures blocking in required GitHub checks
findings.whyItBreaks: GitHub accepts a neutral conclusion for a required status check. When review() throws, this now completes the Needlefish check as neutral, so a PR can satisfy that requirement without completing review. The process exit code still reports failure to the command caller, but it does not change the separately published check.

findings.title: Fetch the patch from the configured GitHub repository
findings.whyItBreaks: The metadata lookup and review publication target GITHUB_REPOSITORY. The new gh pr diff command resolves a bare PR number using GitHub CLI's default repository and runs in the process working directory, ignoring the adapter's cwd. If that default points to another repository with the same PR number, Needlefish can approve the configured PR based on an unrelated patch. If no repository resolves, the command throws before the review error handler.

findings.title: Pin the patch to the commit that receives the review
findings.whyItBreaks: The metadata request snapshots the PR head, while gh pr diff subsequently resolves the PR by number. A push between the two calls can pair the newer patch with the older head SHA. postReview then submits the verdict for the older commit even though Needlefish inspected a different revision.

findings.title: Derive changed paths from the patch under review
findings.whyItBreaks: The patch now comes from the remote PR, while changedFileSet still compares the base SHA with local HEAD. If the PR already contains b.ts and the runner has an older checkout that changes only a.ts, the patch includes b.ts but changedPaths omits it. The inline comment filter then drops any finding on b.ts from the GitHub inline review.

findings.title: Run the reviewer from a trusted checkout
findings.whyItBreaks: The workflow checks out the selected PR SHA and executes its reviewer on a self-hosted runner with a token that can write PR reviews and checks. The manual dispatch path accepts a PR number without enforcing the same-repository restriction. A selected PR that supplies the reviewer can control its own review result and run code with the runner account's access.

findings.title: Install the reviewer from a checkout that contains it
findings.whyItBreaks: The reviewed commit contains only the workflow and .needlefish/answers.json. With the separate tool checkout removed, pnpm install runs in a directory with no package.json or lockfile. The install fails and the review step never runs. The referenced src/cli.ts is also absent.

A PR that supplies the CLI controls the process responsible for reporting its own review and can publish misleading review comments or check results. Moving the install into that checkout leaves pnpm without a package manifest or lockfile, and the subsequent review command has no src/cli.ts to launch. The base workflow obtained those files from a separate reviewer checkout.

findings.title: Preserve case and whitespace normalization for severity labels
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview accepts raw finding entries and passes them directly to normalizeFinding. A severity of ` p0 ` previously became P0 after trimming and uppercasing. The new exact membership check rejects it, and the public review result reports P3, indistinguishable from an explicit P3.

findings.title: Preserve the P1 fallback for missing or invalid severity
findings.whyItBreaks: The public normalizer accepts Partial<Finding>, and normalizeReview permits entries that omit severity. A finding with no severity or an unrecognized value previously received P1. It now receives P3, which lowers its reported priority and makes it indistinguishable from a finding explicitly labeled P3. Restoring case and whitespace normalization alone leaves this regression in place.

findings.title: Preserve severity normalization and the P1 fallback
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview passes raw finding entries directly to normalizeFinding. The base implementation trims and uppercases a severity such as " p0 " and returns P0. The new exact-match check rejects that input and returns P3, which is indistinguishable from an explicitly low-risk finding. Missing and unrecognized severities also fall from P1 to P3.

findings.title: Preserve case and whitespace normalization for severities
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview accepts untyped input and passes each finding to normalizeFinding. A severity of " p0 " previously became P0. The new exact membership check rejects it, and normalizeReview returns the finding as P3.

findings.title: Preserve the P1 fallback for missing or invalid severities
findings.whyItBreaks: Findings with an omitted or unrecognized severity previously reached normalizeReview callers as P1. They now reach callers as P3, the lowest severity, and the returned data provides no way to distinguish them from findings explicitly classified as P3.

findings.title: Keep GitHub tokens out of the Codex review subprocess
findings.whyItBreaks: Deleting the explicit env option makes spawnSync inherit process.env. If the parent sets GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN, or GITHUB_API_TOKEN, the Codex process launched to review repository content receives those credentials. The read-only sandbox argument does not prevent Node from passing them to the child process.

findings.title: Keep GitHub credentials out of the Codex subprocess
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing the explicit env option makes spawnSync inherit process.env. When the review runner has GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN, or GITHUB_API_TOKEN set, the Codex process receives those credentials while handling repository-controlled input. The read-only filesystem setting does not prevent the child process from reading its environment.

findings.title: Keep GitHub tokens out of the Codex subprocess
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing the env option makes spawnSync inherit process.env. If the parent has GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN, or GITHUB_API_TOKEN set, the Codex process receives those credentials when launched to review repository content. The read-only flag is passed to Codex as an argument and does not change which environment variables Node passes to the process.

findings.title: Keep fork PR code off the self-hosted runner
findings.whyItBreaks: The deleted job condition rejected fork PRs before runner assignment. Once GitHub permits a fork PR workflow to run, this job checks out the contributor's head SHA and executes src/cli.ts from that checkout on a self-hosted machine. A read-only fork token still leaves the contributor's code running with the runner account's local permissions.

findings.title: Restore the same-repository check for self-hosted review
findings.whyItBreaks: The deleted job condition excluded heads from other repositories. Once GitHub admits a fork PR run, the job checks out the fork's head, installs from that checkout, and executes its review entry point on the self-hosted runner. A read-only fork token does not restrict what a process can access under the runner's OS account.

findings.title: Restore the same-repository guard on the self-hosted review job
findings.whyItBreaks: The guard deleted at base line 19 skipped the review job when the PR head came from a fork. The job now runs for fork PRs that GitHub permits to run. It checks out the contributor's head SHA and executes src/cli.ts from that checkout on the self-hosted runner, giving contributor-controlled code the runner account's access.

findings.title: Preserve zero for runner cleanup delays
findings.whyItBreaks: Both cleanup environment variables previously accepted `0`, which Node schedules with a 1 ms timer delay. The new predicate substitutes 5000 ms before SIGKILL and 2000 ms before giving up on child close. With both variables set to `0`, a runner that survives SIGTERM and whose pipes stay open after SIGKILL now returns its timeout result roughly seven seconds after the initial timeout fires.

findings.title: Preserve zero-valued runner timeout settings
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous parser accepted an explicit 0 for both timeout settings. The new predicate replaces NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0 with 5,000 ms, delaying SIGKILL for a child that survives SIGTERM. It also replaces NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0 with 2,000 ms, delaying the timeout result when the child's close event stays pending. With both settings at zero, the scheduled post-timeout wait on that path changes from two minimum-delay timers to 7,000 ms.

findings.title: Preserve explicit zero values for runner shutdown delays
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous parser passed an explicit "0" through to Node's minimum timer delay. The new predicate replaces it with 5000 ms for NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS and 2000 ms for NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS. With both settings at zero and no child close event, the runner now takes about seven additional seconds to return ETIMEDOUT.

findings.title: Keep changed files outside the top six hotspots in scope
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed coverage backstop was the only path that added changed files missing from the selected hotspots. If a seventh hotspot is the only one containing a changed file, the deep-review loop never receives that file. The pipeline still submits its partial findings to the critic without an incomplete-coverage signal.

findings.title: Continue reviewing after an individual hotspot fails
findings.whyItBreaks: An exception during a deep pass now rejects the exported review call. For example, if the first hotspot succeeds and JSON extraction throws on the second, the third hotspot and critic never run, and the first hotspot's findings never reach the caller. Previously the failure was recorded as a blocking residual risk and later hotspots were reviewed.

findings.title: Preserve blocking risks reported by deep reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: A successful deep pass can return a blocking residual risk with zero findings. The merge replaces that risk with an empty array, so the critic cannot distinguish it from a review that reported no risk. The verdict and returned risks are then built solely from the critic's output.

findings.title: Preserve distinct findings that share a title prefix
findings.whyItBreaks: Two findings at the same file and starting line with the same category and normalized 60-character title prefix now share a key even when they describe different failures. At equal severity, the second finding is discarded before the critic sees it. The base key distinguished findings whose explanations differed within the first 80 normalized characters.

findings.title: Preserve the caller's focus in large reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: The patch removes focus from the map bundle and deletes the focus substitution between the hotspot and base substitutions. With a nonempty focus and 11 changed files, review() selects the large-review path. The map prompt receives no focus field, and the hotspot prompt construction never reads the supplied value. The same value is included in the full bundle sent by the small-review path.

findings.title: Preserve caller focus in large-review prompts
findings.whyItBreaks: A bundle with 11 changed files and focus set to "authorization" enters reviewLarge. The map prompt now receives JSON with no focus field, and the per-hotspot prompt no longer substitutes the supplied focus. The large-review pipeline therefore loses the caller’s requested emphasis at both stages. The small-review path still forwards the full bundle.

findings.title: Preserve the requested focus in large reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: For a bundle with 11 changed files and focus set to "authorization", the base code sends the focus in the map bundle and substitutes it into each hotspot prompt. The revised code omits it from the map bundle at lines 83–89 and removes the hotspot substitution, so both stages receive the same inputs as a review with no focus. Small reviews still serialize the full bundle.

findings.title: Carry rounded seconds into the minutes field
findings.whyItBreaks: The formatter calculates minutes before rounding seconds. At 119,500 ms it calculates 1 minute and rounds the remaining 59.5 seconds to 60, so both per-call and total timings can display `1m 60s`. The base formatter displays `2m 0s` for the same input.

findings.title: Round the full duration before splitting minutes and seconds
findings.whyItBreaks: The formatter floors minutes before rounding the remaining seconds, so the rounded remainder can reach 60 without incrementing the minutes. A duration of 119500 ms now renders as `1m 60s` instead of `2m 0s`. Both per-call timings and the total use this formatter.

findings.title: Carry rounded seconds into the minutes field
findings.whyItBreaks: The formatter floors the minutes before rounding the remainder. At 119,500 ms it renders `1m 60s`, while the base revision renders `2m 0s`. The same regression affects both per-call and total durations in the review footer.

findings.title: Reject zero in parsePositiveInteger
findings.whyItBreaks: Number("0") and Number("") both yield 0. The new guard lets that value through, so the exported parser returns 0 where callers previously received a validation error and were guaranteed a positive integer on success.

findings.title: Reject zero in parsePositiveInteger
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported parser promises a positive integer. Number("0"), Number(""), and Number(" ") all produce 0. The old guard threw for each input. The new guard returns 0 as a successful result.

findings.title: Reject zero in the positive-integer parser
findings.whyItBreaks: Number converts "0", "", and whitespace-only strings to 0. The new guard accepts 0 and returns it, so callers receive zero where the exported API promises a positive integer and previously threw a validation error.
